chapters.customSummary:
- A WHERE clause is a business rule written as a predicate; say the rule in plain English first and check each word maps to a condition.
- Put one condition per line, use parentheses when mixing AND/OR, and prefer IN over long OR chains (watch NOT IN with NULLs).
- BETWEEN is inclusive, and boundary tests need > vs >= verified at exactly the boundary value.
- Date filters: half-open ranges (>= start AND < next_start), relative dates differ by dialect, freeze the date for repeatable tests.
- Avoid wrapping columns in functions (YEAR(col) = 2025); use ranges so indexes can be used (sargable).
- Mirror UI filters in SQL and compare the list of IDs, not just counts.
- Partition check: bucket counts should sum to the total, otherwise rows fall through a gap.
- Optional-filter query pattern (:param IS NULL OR col = :param) tells you what combinations to test.
- Common mistakes: missing soft-delete filter, wrong case/whitespace, unparenthesized OR, = NULL, wrong environment.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## A WHERE clause is a business rule written as a condition
In Part 1 you learned the operators. Here the skill is translating a requirement into a predicate that selects exactly the right rows. "Show me leave that still needs a manager's attention" becomes status = 'pending'. "Employees who can currently log in" becomes status = 'active' AND is_deleted = 0. Most wrong test results don't come from syntax errors but from a predicate that is almost the business rule: a missing is_deleted = 0, a > where the requirement says "at least", an OR that swallowed an AND. Before you run any query, say the rule out loud in plain English, then check that every word in the sentence has a matching piece in the WHERE.
## Combining many conditions
Real filters stack conditions across several columns. Group with parentheses so the intent is unmistakable:
-- Approved or pending leave, longer than 2 days, starting after 1 Oct 2026
```sql
SELECT leave_request_id, employee_id, days, status, start_date
FROM   leave_requests
WHERE  status IN ('approved', 'pending')
  AND  days > 2
  AND  start_date >= '2026-10-01';
```

leave_request_id | employee_id | days | status  | start_date
1                | 2           | 3    | pending | 2026-10-05
4                | 3           | 6    | pending | 2026-12-24

Layout is a real defence here. One condition per line, AND/OR at the start of the line, and each rule separately commentable. When a query returns something odd, you can comment out one line at a time and watch which condition changes the result. That is the SQL equivalent of removing one filter at a time in a Playwright locator chain to find which part stopped matching.
## IN and NOT IN with lists
IN compares a column against a list, and NOT IN is its negation. They beat chains of OR:
WHERE department_id IN (1, 3)
-- same as: department_id = 1 OR department_id = 3

Two cautions. First, NOT IN breaks when the list contains NULL, as chapter 2.3 shows in detail. Second, some databases cap the list length or slow down badly with very long lists; a 5,000-item IN is a signal to use a join or a temp table instead (Part 4). MySQL and PostgreSQL also support row-value comparison, which filters on pairs of columns at once:
-- Match two specific (employee, date) pairs
```sql
SELECT * FROM attendance
WHERE (employee_id, work_date) IN ((1, '2026-09-14'), (2, '2026-09-14'));
```

This works in MySQL and PostgreSQL but not in older SQL Server versions, where you'd use OR groups instead.
## Numeric and range filters
BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends, so days BETWEEN 2 AND 6 returns 2, 6 and everything between. For boundary testing, always write down which side of the boundary each value should fall on, then verify with queries at exactly the boundary:
```sql
SELECT leave_request_id, days FROM leave_requests WHERE days >= 6;   -- includes 6
SELECT leave_request_id, days FROM leave_requests WHERE days >  6;   -- excludes 6
```

If a business rule says "leave of 6 days or more needs HR approval", the first query returns your test population, and the app's behaviour at exactly 6 days should agree with it.

| Date filters | Dates are where most filtering bugs live. Some reliable patterns: |
|---|---|
| -- Exact date (a DATE column) | WHERE work_date = '2026-09-14' |

-- A whole month, using a half-open range (safe for DATE and DATETIME columns alike)
WHERE created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01'

-- Relative: last 30 days
```sql
-- MySQL
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 30 DAY
-- PostgreSQL
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
-- SQL Server
WHERE created_at >= DATEADD(day, -30, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE))
```

Relative filters change every day, which makes them awkward for repeatable tests. When you're validating a "Last 30 Days" report, freeze the date by using a literal ('2026-09-20' - INTERVAL 30 DAY) and set the app's test clock to match if it lets you.
## Don't wrap the column in a function (sargability)
A filter is sargable if the database can use an index to find matching rows quickly. Wrapping the column in a function usually defeats the index:
-- Slow shape: the function runs on every row, index can't be used
WHERE YEAR(hire_date) = 2025

-- Fast shape: a plain range on the raw column
## WHERE hire_date >= '2025-01-01' AND hire_date < '2026-01-01'

Both return the same rows. On our five-row table it doesn't matter, but on a 5-million-row attendance table the first version can be the reason a saved sanity check takes minutes. It's also a hint about the app: if a report is slow, developers may have written the first form. Chapter 8.5 returns to this with EXPLAIN.
## Filters that mirror the UI
Most list screens in an app are a table plus filters: status, department, date range, search text. Each filter becomes a WHERE condition, and the combination of filters becomes AND. Testing them means running the same combination in SQL and comparing counts and IDs with what the UI shows.
```ts
test('active QA employees filter matches DB', async ({ page }) => {
| await page.goto('/employees'); | await page.getByLabel('Department').selectOption('QA'); |
|---|---|
| await page.getByLabel('Status').selectOption('active'); | await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Apply' }).click(); |
```

```ts
  const uiEmails = (await page.locator('td.email').allInnerTexts()).sort();
```

```ts
  const [rows]: any = await db.execute(
| `SELECT e.email FROM employees e | JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id |
|---|---|
| WHERE d.name = ? AND e.status = ? AND e.is_deleted = 0 | ORDER BY e.email`, ['QA', 'active']); |
```

  expect(uiEmails).toEqual(rows.map((r: any) => r.email));
});

Comparing the list of IDs (or emails) is stronger than comparing counts. Two wrong rows can cancel out into the right count. Chapter 9.5 builds this into a full pagination, sorting and filter validation approach.
## The partition check
When a filter splits data into buckets (status is one of a fixed set), the buckets should add up to the whole. If they don't, some rows fall through a gap:
```sql
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE is_deleted = 0)                         AS total,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE is_deleted = 0 AND status = 'active')   AS active_cnt,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE is_deleted = 0 AND status = 'inactive') AS inactive_cnt,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE is_deleted = 0 AND status = 'resigned') AS resigned_cnt;
```

total | active_cnt | inactive_cnt | resigned_cnt
4     | 3          | 0            | 1

3 + 0 + 1 = 4, so no row is stranded. If the sum were 3, a row with an unexpected or NULL status would be invisible in every tab of the UI, which is exactly the kind of data bug users report as "my employee disappeared."
Optional filters, as backends implement them
| Developers often write a single query where each filter is optional: | SELECT * FROM employees |
|---|---|
| WHERE (:status IS NULL OR status = :status) | AND (:dept   IS NULL OR department_id = :dept); |

If a parameter is NULL, that filter is skipped. As a tester, this tells you what to try: every filter alone, every pair, all filters, none, and empty-string vs missing parameters (which may or may not be converted to NULL).
## Mistakes to check for in your own WHERE clauses
Forgot the soft-delete or tenant filter the app applies (is_deleted = 0, company_id = ...).
Compared to the wrong case or spacing ('Active' vs 'active'); see 2.5.
Mixed AND/OR without parentheses.
Used BETWEEN on a DATETIME column with a bare date as the end.
Filtered on = NULL instead of IS NULL.
Tested on the wrong environment, so zero rows came back for a perfectly good query.

chapters.title: 2.2 ORDER BY, LIMIT/TOP, DISTINCT
chapters.overviewText: This is worth repeating from Part 1, because it's the root of many flaky database assertions. A table has no inherent order. The database returns rows in whatever way is cheapest at that moment, which can change after an insert, a vacuum, or a different execution plan. Any test that says "the first row should be X" needs an ORDER BY. In UI terms, it's the equivalent of asserting on nth(0) of a list that has no guaranteed sort. ASC (ascending) is the default and DESC reverses it. You can sort by a column that isn't in the SELECT list, and (unlike WHERE) you can use a SELECT alias in ORDER BY, because sorting happens after the select step in the logical order from Part 1.
chapters.why: 2.2 ORDER BY, LIMIT/TOP, DISTINCT is how a tester proves stored state, not just the screen. This is worth repeating from Part 1, because it's the root of many flaky database assertions.
chapters.when: Open this chapter when you are on the Filtering & Sorting path and need ORDER BY, LIMIT/TOP, DISTINCT against the hrms_practice schema, a shared QA database, or a Bizlevate HRMS screen.

practical.scenario: A leave, payroll, attendance, or appointment check depends on ORDER BY, LIMIT/TOP, DISTINCT.
practical.pass: You apply ORDER BY, LIMIT/TOP, DISTINCT on the sample database (or a tagged QA row) and can say what empty vs non-empty results mean.
practical.fail: You copy a blog query, skip ORDER BY, LIMIT/TOP, DISTINCT, or treat a UI success toast as proof the row is correct.

chapters.customSummary:
- No ORDER BY means no guaranteed order; never assert on "first row" without one.
- Multi-column sort applies left to right; use CASE in ORDER BY for custom business order.
- NULL placement: MySQL/SQL Server put NULLs first on ASC, PostgreSQL puts them last.
- Text sort follows collation; UI (JS) and DB sorting can legitimately disagree, so decide the source of truth.
- Row limiting: LIMIT (MySQL/PG), TOP or OFFSET ... FETCH (SQL Server), FETCH FIRST (standard).
- "Latest row" pattern: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1, filtered by something unique to your test.
- Pagination: OFFSET = (page - 1) * page_size; sort must be total, so add the primary key as the final tiebreaker.
- DISTINCT dedupes whole rows and COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique values; don't use it to hide duplicate-producing joins.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Without ORDER BY, the order is not defined
This is worth repeating from Part 1, because it's the root of many flaky database assertions. A table has no inherent order. The database returns rows in whatever way is cheapest at that moment, which can change after an insert, a vacuum, or a different execution plan. Any test that says "the first row should be X" needs an ORDER BY. In UI terms, it's the equivalent of asserting on nth(0) of a list that has no guaranteed sort.

| Sorting basics | SELECT first_name, hire_date |
|---|---|
| FROM   employees | ORDER  BY hire_date DESC; |

| first_name \| hire_date | Bikash     \| 2025-09-01 | Ravi       \| 2025-03-10 |
|---|---|---|
| Asha       \| 2024-03-01 | Mina       \| 2023-07-15 | Sita       \| 2022-01-20 |

ASC (ascending) is the default and DESC reverses it. You can sort by a column that isn't in the SELECT list, and (unlike WHERE) you can use a SELECT alias in ORDER BY, because sorting happens after the select step in the logical order from Part 1.
## Sorting by several columns
Sort keys apply left to right; later keys only break ties in earlier ones:
```sql
SELECT first_name, department_id, hire_date
FROM   employees
ORDER  BY department_id ASC, hire_date DESC;
```

| first_name \| department_id \| hire_date | Mina       \| 1             \| 2023-07-15 | Bikash     \| 2             \| 2025-09-01 |
|---|---|---|
| Ravi       \| 2             \| 2025-03-10 | Asha       \| 2             \| 2024-03-01 | Sita       \| 3             \| 2022-01-20 |

You can also sort by position (ORDER BY 2, 3) but that breaks silently when someone reorders the select list; prefer names.
## Custom sort orders with CASE
If the UI shows statuses in a business order (pending first, then approved, then everything else), the plain alphabetical sort won't match. The database version uses CASE (chapter 2.4):

| SELECT leave_request_id, status | FROM   leave_requests |
|---|---|
| ORDER  BY CASE status WHEN 'pending' THEN 1 WHEN 'approved' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END, | leave_request_id; |

## Where NULLs land differs by database
When the sort column has NULLs, the position of those rows depends on the dialect:

| Database | ORDER BY col ASC puts NULLs | ORDER BY col DESC puts NULLs | MySQL | First | Last |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SQL Server | First | Last | PostgreSQL | Last | First |

## Sorting our employees by manager_id ASC, employee_id ASC:
MySQL / SQL Server:  1, 3, 4 (manager_id NULL), then 2, 5 (manager_id 1)
## PostgreSQL:          2, 5 (manager_id 1), then 1, 3, 4 (NULL)

PostgreSQL lets you override with ORDER BY manager_id NULLS FIRST; in MySQL you can force NULLs last with ORDER BY manager_id IS NULL, manager_id. If a UI shows "no manager" rows at the top of a sorted list, first find out which behaviour the requirement expects before calling it a bug.
## Text sorting depends on collation
Text sorting follows the column's collation (chapter 2.5). Case, accents and punctuation can rank differently in the database and in the front end. A UI that sorts with JavaScript localeCompare may disagree with a database that uses a binary or case-sensitive collation. Two typical false alarms: "apple" vs "Banana" ordering, and names with accents. When comparing UI order with ORDER BY output, agree on the source of truth first.
```ts
test('name column sorted ascending matches DB order', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.getByRole('columnheader', { name: 'Name' }).click();
  const uiNames = await page.locator('td.name').allInnerTexts();
```

```ts
  const [rows]: any = await db.execute(
    'SELECT first_name FROM employees WHERE is_deleted = 0 ORDER BY first_name ASC, employee_id ASC');
```

  expect(uiNames).toEqual(rows.map((r: any) => r.first_name));
});

## Limiting rows
Every dialect can cut the result to the first N rows, but the syntax differs:

| Dialect | First 3 rows | Skip 2, take 3 (pagination) | MySQL | ... LIMIT 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ... LIMIT 3 OFFSET 2 | PostgreSQL | ... LIMIT 3 | ... LIMIT 3 OFFSET 2 | SQL Server |
| SELECT TOP 3 ... | ... ORDER BY x OFFSET 2 ROWS FETCH NEXT 3 ROWS ONLY | Standard SQL | ... FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY | ... OFFSET 2 ROWS FETCH NEXT 3 ROWS ONLY |

LIMIT without ORDER BY gives you an arbitrary N rows, which is fine for a quick peek and wrong for any assertion.
## The "row my test just created" pattern
The most common tester use of ORDER BY plus LIMIT is fetching the newest row after a UI or API action:

| SELECT * FROM leave_requests | WHERE  employee_id = 2 |
|---|---|
| ORDER  BY created_at DESC, leave_request_id DESC | LIMIT  1; |

Notice the tie-breaker (leave_request_id DESC). Two rows created in the same second have the same created_at, and without a tiebreaker either could come first. In shared databases, also filter by something unique to your test (your test user, your tagged email) so you don't pick up someone else's newer row.
## Pagination and the stable-sort rule
A list screen showing 2 rows per page turns into LIMIT 2 OFFSET 0 for page 1, LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2 for page 2, and so on. The formula is OFFSET = (page - 1) * page_size. Page 2 of our employees sorted by ID:
```sql
SELECT employee_id, first_name FROM employees
ORDER BY employee_id
LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2;
```

employee_id | first_name
3           | Mina
4           | Sita

Pagination is only correct if the sort order is total, meaning no two rows compare equal. Sorting by hire_date alone is unsafe if two people share a hire date, because the database can order the tied rows differently for page 1 and page 2, so a row appears on both pages or on neither. The fix is always to add a unique column as the last sort key (usually the primary key). That's one of the top pagination defects to test, and chapter 9.5 covers how.
Also know that a huge OFFSET gets slow (the database still walks past every skipped row), and that inserting a row while someone pages through can shift rows between pages. Both are behaviours worth noting but not usually bugs.
DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows
```sql
SELECT DISTINCT status FROM employees;
```

| status | active |
|---|---|
| resigned | inactive |

DISTINCT applies to the entire selected row, not just the first column. SELECT DISTINCT department_id, status returns each unique pair. You can also count unique values:

| SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_total, | COUNT(DISTINCT department_id) AS departments_used |
|---|---|
| FROM   employees; | -- 5 and 3 |

## DISTINCT can hide bugs
Adding DISTINCT to make a query "look right" is dangerous for testers. If a join produces duplicated rows and you tack on DISTINCT, the duplicates vanish from your result while the underlying problem (a bad join, or duplicate records in the table) remains. When you are hunting duplicates, do the opposite: don't use DISTINCT, and group by the supposed-unique key and count (chapter 3.2 and 6.3). Use DISTINCT deliberately, to answer "which distinct values exist?" (for example, to list every status value actually in use and compare it against the documented list).
```sql
SELECT DISTINCT and GROUP BY overlap, but GROUP BY also lets you aggregate, which Part 3 covers.
```

chapters.title: 2.3 NULL Handling
chapters.overviewText: NULL marks a value that is missing or unknown. It is not 0, not '' (an empty string), and not the text 'NULL'. Those four are all different: A leave request's approved_by is NULL while pending: no approver yet. A days value of 0 would say "zero days of leave," a completely different statement. These distinctions matter for testing because apps are often inconsistent. The UI form might save a blank optional field as '', while the API (when the field is omitted) saves NULL. Both look blank on screen, but they behave differently in queries and reports. Test both paths, then look at the raw data.
chapters.why: 2.3 NULL Handling is how a tester proves stored state, not just the screen. NULL marks a value that is missing or unknown.

chapters.customSummary:
- NULL = unknown; it differs from 0, '' and 'NULL', and UI vs API paths may store '' vs NULL.
- Comparisons with NULL are UNKNOWN and WHERE drops those rows; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, never = NULL.
- col <> 1 drops rows where col is NULL; add OR col IS NULL or use a NULL-safe operator (<=> in MySQL, IS DISTINCT FROM in PG/SQL Server 2022).
- NOT IN with a NULL in the list or subquery returns nothing; use NOT IN (... WHERE x IS NOT NULL) or NOT EXISTS.
- Arithmetic with NULL is NULL, and CONCAT with NULL differs by dialect (NULL in MySQL, ignored in PG/SQL Server).
- COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) counts non-NULLs; aggregates ignore NULLs.
- UNIQUE and NULL: multiple NULLs allowed in MySQL/PG, only one in SQL Server.
- Every nullable column is a test case; every NOT NULL column is a negative test.
- Violation queries: approved leave without approver, checkout without check-in, missing check-out on past dates.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## NULL means "no value", not zero and not empty
NULL marks a value that is missing or unknown. It is not 0, not '' (an empty string), and not the text 'NULL'. Those four are all different:

| Stored value | Meaning | IS NULL? | = ''? | NULL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| No value / unknown | Yes | Unknown | '' | A known, empty string |
| No | Yes | 0 | The number zero | No |
| (type issue) | 'NULL' | The four-letter word | No | No |

A leave request's approved_by is NULL while pending: no approver yet. A days value of 0 would say "zero days of leave," a completely different statement. These distinctions matter for testing because apps are often inconsistent. The UI form might save a blank optional field as '', while the API (when the field is omitted) saves NULL. Both look blank on screen, but they behave differently in queries and reports. Test both paths, then look at the raw data.
## Three-valued logic
Because NULL means "unknown," comparing anything to it yields UNKNOWN, not true or false. WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE, so UNKNOWN rows are silently dropped. The rules:

| A | B |
|---|---|
| A AND B | A OR B |
| TRUE | UNKNOWN |
| UNKNOWN | TRUE |
| FALSE | UNKNOWN |
| FALSE | UNKNOWN |
| UNKNOWN | UNKNOWN |
| UNKNOWN | UNKNOWN |

And NOT UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN. The everyday consequence is that NULL = NULL isn't true, and NULL <> 5 isn't true either.
Testing for NULL: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
```sql
SELECT first_name FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL;
```

| first_name | Asha |
|---|---|
| Mina | Sita |

Writing WHERE manager_id = NULL returns zero rows, no error, which is why it's such a stubborn beginner bug. Any time a query returns nothing when you expected something, check whether you compared to NULL with =.
The "not equal" trap
```sql
SELECT first_name FROM employees WHERE manager_id <> 1;
```

You'd expect Asha, Mina and Sita, the employees whose manager isn't employee 1. You get zero rows. Their manager_id is NULL, and NULL <> 1 is UNKNOWN, so they're dropped. Correct versions:
WHERE manager_id <> 1 OR manager_id IS NULL

```sql
-- MySQL's NULL-safe operator:
WHERE NOT (manager_id <=> 1)
```

```sql
-- PostgreSQL / SQL Server 2022+:
WHERE manager_id IS DISTINCT FROM 1
```

Whenever a column is nullable, a negative filter (<>, NOT IN, NOT LIKE) needs an explicit decision about NULL.
## The NOT IN trap
This one bites experienced people. Suppose you want employees who don't manage anyone:
```sql
SELECT first_name
FROM   employees
WHERE  employee_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees);
```

Expected: Ravi, Mina, Sita, Bikash. Actual: no rows. The subquery returns {NULL, 1, NULL, NULL, 1}. For any employee, employee_id NOT IN (NULL, 1) expands to employee_id <> NULL AND employee_id <> 1. The first part is UNKNOWN, so the whole condition can never be TRUE. The fixes:
-- 1: exclude NULLs from the subquery
WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL)

-- 2: use NOT EXISTS (5.1), which handles NULLs sensibly
## WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees m WHERE m.manager_id = employees.employee_id)

This is important in orphan-record checks (6.3), where "rows in table A with no match in table B" is written with NOT IN, and where one stray NULL in B makes your check report "no problems found" when there are plenty.
## NULL and arithmetic or string operations
Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: 5 + NULL is NULL. If allowances were nullable, then basic_salary + allowances - deductions becomes NULL for every employee who has a blank allowance, and your comparison with net_pay silently doesn't flag them. String concatenation is dialect-dependent:

| Expression | MySQL | PostgreSQL | SQL Server |
|---|---|---|---|
| CONCAT('a', NULL) | NULL | 'a' | 'a' |
| 'a' \|\| NULL / 'a' + NULL | (n/a) | NULL | NULL |
| CONCAT_WS(' ', 'a', NULL, 'b') | 'a b' (skips NULL) | 'a b' | 'a b' |

So "full name" columns built with CONCAT(first, ' ', middle, ' ', last) show NULL in MySQL for everyone without a middle name. You'll see it on exports and reports as blank names, so watch for it. COALESCE (2.4) is the usual fix.

| NULL in aggregates and sorting | Aggregates ignore NULLs (except COUNT(*)): |
|---|---|
| SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(manager_id) AS with_manager FROM employees; | -- 5 and 2 |

COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts rows where that column is not NULL. Use the wrong one and your count is off by however many blanks exist. Part 3 expands on this. For sorting, see the NULL placement table in 2.2.
## NULL and uniqueness / constraints
A UNIQUE column can normally hold several NULLs in MySQL and PostgreSQL (since NULL is never equal to another NULL), but SQL Server treats them as equal and allows only one. So the same schema can accept two employees with no national ID on one database and reject the second on another. A NOT NULL column can't hold NULL at all. When you read a schema, note which columns are NOT NULL, because each nullable column is a test case ("what happens when this is blank?") and each NOT NULL column is a negative test ("what happens if the API omits it?").
Violation queries built on NULL
-- Approved leave that has no approver
```sql
SELECT leave_request_id FROM leave_requests
WHERE status = 'approved' AND approved_by IS NULL;          -- expect 0 rows
```

-- Checked out but never checked in (impossible)
```sql
SELECT attendance_id, employee_id, work_date FROM attendance
WHERE check_in IS NULL AND check_out IS NOT NULL;           -- returns employee 3, 14 Sep
```

-- Checked in but no check-out on a past date
```sql
SELECT attendance_id, employee_id, work_date FROM attendance
WHERE check_in IS NOT NULL AND check_out IS NULL
  AND work_date < CURRENT_DATE;                             -- returns employee 2, 14 Sep
```

The middle query returns a row that is a genuine anomaly, an impossible punch pair, so it's a bug-report candidate. The last one is often expected behaviour (people forget to check out) but may violate a rule like "system auto-closes open attendance at midnight." Decide, based on the requirement, whether it's a defect. Chapter 10.3 collects attendance templates like these.

chapters.title: 2.4 Functions & Expressions (CASE, COALESCE, NULLIF, string/date functions, ROUND/CAST, GROUP_CONCAT/STRING_AGG)
chapters.overviewText: Almost anywhere a column name can go (SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY), you can put an expression: arithmetic, function calls, CASE. For a tester this is what turns SQL from "show me the rows" into "independently compute what the answer should be and compare it to what the app stored." Most functions differ in name and behaviour between MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server, so this chapter groups them by task and flags the differences. Appendix B has the compact version. CASE returns a value based on conditions. It comes in two forms. The simple form compares one expression against values:
chapters.why: 2.4 Functions & Expressions (CASE, COALESCE, NULLIF, string/date functions, ROUND/CAST, GROUP_CONCAT/STRING_AGG) is how a tester proves stored state, not just the screen. chapters.customSummary:
- CASE: simple and searched forms, first match wins, no ELSE gives NULL; use for labels, expected values and conditional counts (SUM(CASE ...)).
- COALESCE gives the first non-NULL and protects calculations from nullable inputs (IFNULL/ISNULL are dialect-specific).
- NULLIF(a, b) avoids divide-by-zero and converts blanks to NULL.
- String functions differ: LENGTH is bytes in MySQL but characters in PG, LEN in SQL Server ignores trailing spaces; use character-length functions for max-length tests.
- Date functions differ, especially DATEDIFF argument order (MySQL end, start vs SQL Server day, start, end); leave days need + 1 for inclusive ranges and business-calendar rules.
- Month-end arithmetic clamps (31 Jan + 1 month = 28 Feb); test 29/30/31.
- Rounding differs across SQL (half away from zero), Python round() (half to even) and JS Math.round(); compute expected values with the rule from the requirement.
- Integer division truncates in PG/SQL Server (7/2 = 3), but not in MySQL; cast to decimal and test values that leave remainders.
- CAST converts types deliberately; failed casts warn in MySQL and error elsewhere.
- GROUP_CONCAT (MySQL) / STRING_AGG (PG, SQL Server) collapse rows to text; specify inner ordering, and beware MySQL's 1024-character default truncation.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Expressions let the query do the calculating
Almost anywhere a column name can go (SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY), you can put an expression: arithmetic, function calls, CASE. For a tester this is what turns SQL from "show me the rows" into "independently compute what the answer should be and compare it to what the app stored." Most functions differ in name and behaviour between MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server, so this chapter groups them by task and flags the differences. Appendix B has the compact version.
## CASE: if/else inside SQL
CASE returns a value based on conditions. It comes in two forms. The simple form compares one expression against values:

| SELECT leave_request_id, status, | CASE status | WHEN 'pending'  THEN 'Awaiting action' | WHEN 'approved' THEN 'Granted' |
|---|---|---|---|
| WHEN 'rejected' THEN 'Declined' | ELSE 'Other' | END AS status_label | FROM leave_requests; |

The searched form evaluates independent conditions, which lets you use ranges and multiple columns:
```sql
SELECT leave_request_id, days,
```
| CASE | WHEN days >= 6 THEN 'Long (needs HR)' | WHEN days >= 3 THEN 'Medium' |
|---|---|---|
| ELSE 'Short' | END AS leave_band | FROM leave_requests; |

leave_request_id | days | leave_band
| 1                \| 3    \| Medium | 2                \| 1    \| Short |
|---|---|
| 3                \| 2    \| Short | 4                \| 6    \| Long (needs HR) |

Three behaviours to remember. CASE checks conditions top to bottom and the first match wins, so order matters when ranges overlap. If nothing matches and there's no ELSE, the result is NULL, and a missing ELSE is a quiet source of blank cells. All branches should return compatible types (all text or all numbers). Testers use CASE in three main ways: labelling data to compare with what the UI displays, encoding a business rule as an expected value, and building conditional counts:
```sql
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'pending'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pending_cnt,
```
| SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS approved_cnt, | SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'rejected' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS rejected_cnt |
|---|---|
| FROM leave_requests; | -- 2, 1, 1 |

That one query produces every dashboard tile count at once, which is handy for validating the leave dashboard against the database (9.6). SUM and grouping are explained in Part 3; here focus on the CASE piece.
## COALESCE: first non-NULL value
COALESCE(a, b, c, ...) returns the first argument that isn't NULL. It's the standard way to give NULL a default, and it works on all three databases:
```sql
SELECT first_name, COALESCE(manager_id, 0) AS manager_ref FROM employees;
```

| first_name \| manager_ref | Asha       \| 0 | Ravi       \| 1 |
|---|---|---|
| Mina       \| 0 | Sita       \| 0 | Bikash     \| 1 |

Its most important job in testing is protecting calculations from nullable inputs:
-- If allowances / deductions could be NULL:
```sql
SELECT employee_id,
       basic_salary + COALESCE(allowances, 0) - COALESCE(deductions, 0) AS expected_net
FROM   payroll;
```

Without COALESCE, one NULL component turns the whole sum into NULL, and your check reports nothing even though the pay is wrong. It's also how you compare two values that might both be missing. Since NULL = NULL isn't true, an expected-vs-actual comparison of nullable columns should be written like COALESCE(a.value, '') = COALESCE(b.value, '') or with a NULL-safe operator (Part 6). MySQL also has IFNULL(x, y), SQL Server has ISNULL(x, y), and PostgreSQL has neither; COALESCE is the portable one.
## NULLIF: turn a specific value into NULL
NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a = b, otherwise a. It has two classic uses. The first is dodging divide-by-zero, since dividing by NULL gives NULL instead of an error:
```sql
SELECT total_amount / NULLIF(working_days, 0) AS daily_rate FROM some_table;
```

The second is cleaning blank strings so they compare as NULL:
```sql
SELECT NULLIF(TRIM(''), '');      -- NULL
SELECT NULLIF(TRIM('  '), '');    -- NULL (only spaces)
```

That is handy when data comes from a UI (which saves '') and an API (which saves NULL) and you want one consistent comparison.

| String functions | Task | MySQL | PostgreSQL | SQL Server |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Join text | CONCAT(a, b) | a \|\| b or CONCAT(a, b) | CONCAT(a, b) or a + b | Join with separator |
| CONCAT_WS(' ', a, b) | CONCAT_WS(' ', a, b) | CONCAT_WS(' ', a, b) | Upper / lower case | UPPER(x), LOWER(x) |
| same | same | Trim spaces | TRIM(x), LTRIM, RTRIM | same |
| TRIM(x) (2017+), LTRIM, RTRIM | Length in characters | CHAR_LENGTH(x) | LENGTH(x) | LEN(x) (ignores trailing spaces!) |
| Length in bytes | LENGTH(x) | OCTET_LENGTH(x) | DATALENGTH(x) | Substring |
| SUBSTRING(x, 2, 3) | SUBSTRING(x, 2, 3) | SUBSTRING(x, 2, 3) | First / last n chars | LEFT(x, n), RIGHT(x, n) |
| same | same | Replace | REPLACE(x, 'a', 'b') | same |
| same | Position of text | LOCATE('@', x) | POSITION('@' IN x) | CHARINDEX('@', x) |

The LENGTH row is the trap. In MySQL, LENGTH('Rávi') returns 5 (bytes) while CHAR_LENGTH('Rávi') returns 4. In PostgreSQL, LENGTH counts characters. SQL Server's LEN('Ravi ') returns 4 because it ignores trailing spaces. When you test "max 50 characters" against the column, use the character-counting function or you'll misjudge non-English names (a Devanagari character takes 3 bytes in UTF-8, so a 20-character Nepali name looks like 60 with MySQL's LENGTH).

| Extracting the domain from an email is a good example of dialect drift: | -- MySQL |
|---|---|
| SELECT SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1) AS domain FROM employees; | -- PostgreSQL |
| SELECT SPLIT_PART(email, '@', 2) AS domain FROM employees; | -- SQL Server |

```sql
Use it to sanity-check data, for example flagging any employee whose email domain isn't the company's. Another common check compares email to LOWER(email) to catch mixed-case entries that might slip past a case-sensitive unique index:
SELECT employee_id, email FROM employees WHERE email <> LOWER(email);
```

Date and time functions

| Task | MySQL | PostgreSQL | SQL Server |
|---|---|---|---|
| Today (date) | CURRENT_DATE | CURRENT_DATE | CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE) |
| Now | NOW() | NOW() | GETDATE() |
| Add 7 days | DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 7 DAY) | d + INTERVAL '7 days' | DATEADD(day, 7, d) |
| Days between | DATEDIFF(end, start) | end - start (dates) | DATEDIFF(day, start, end) |
| Year part | YEAR(d) or EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d) | EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d) | YEAR(d) |
| Format as text | DATE_FORMAT(d, '%Y-%m') | TO_CHAR(d, 'YYYY-MM') | FORMAT(d, 'yyyy-MM') |

Watch the argument order. MySQL's DATEDIFF(a, b) is a - b, while SQL Server's DATEDIFF(day, start, end) is end - start. Copy a query between them without checking and every result flips sign.

| Two worked examples on our data. First, tenure as of a fixed date: | SELECT first_name, hire_date, |
|---|---|
| TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, hire_date, '2026-09-20') AS years_of_service | FROM   employees; |

| first_name \| hire_date  \| years_of_service | Asha       \| 2024-03-01 \| 2 | Ravi       \| 2025-03-10 \| 1 |
|---|---|---|
| Mina       \| 2023-07-15 \| 3 | Sita       \| 2022-01-20 \| 4 | Bikash     \| 2025-09-01 \| 0 |

(SQL Server: DATEDIFF(year, hire_date, '2026-09-20') counts calendar-year boundaries crossed rather than complete years, so it gives different answers. Never assume two functions with the same name measure the same thing.)
Second, verifying stored leave days against calendar days:
```sql
SELECT leave_request_id, start_date, end_date, days AS stored_days,
       DATEDIFF(end_date, start_date) + 1 AS calendar_days
FROM   leave_requests;
```

leave_request_id | start_date | end_date   | stored_days | calendar_days
| 1                \| 2026-10-05 \| 2026-10-07 \| 3           \| 3 | 2                \| 2026-09-15 \| 2026-09-15 \| 1           \| 1 |
|---|---|
| 3                \| 2026-08-31 \| 2026-09-01 \| 2           \| 2 | 4                \| 2026-12-24 \| 2026-12-31 \| 6           \| 8 |

The + 1 makes the range inclusive (5 to 7 October is three days, not two, which is an off-by-one you'll see in a lot of date-difference code). Row 4 differs: 8 calendar days but 6 stored. In this sample data that's because two weekend days fall in the range, so the app counts working days only. That means your "expected" query needs the company's weekend and holiday rules, not just date subtraction. Chapter 10.4 deals with this properly.
Also beware month-end arithmetic: adding one month to 31 January doesn't produce 31 February. DATE_ADD('2026-01-31', INTERVAL 1 MONTH) gives 2026-02-28. Probation-end dates, payroll cycles and subscription renewals all hit this, so include 29, 30 and 31 as start dates in tests.
For attendance, hours worked is a time difference (MySQL shown):
```sql
SELECT employee_id, work_date,
```
| TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in) AS worked, | ROUND(TIME_TO_SEC(TIMEDIFF(check_out, check_in)) / 3600, 2) AS worked_hours |
|---|---|
| FROM   attendance | WHERE  check_in IS NOT NULL AND check_out IS NOT NULL; |

employee_id | work_date  | worked   | worked_hours
1           | 2026-09-14 | 08:29:00 | 8.48

PostgreSQL gets the same interval with check_out - check_in, and SQL Server with DATEDIFF(MINUTE, check_in, check_out). Rows with a NULL on either side yield NULL, which is why the WHERE filters them out. It's also a reminder that attendance across midnight (a night shift checking out at 02:00) needs date-time columns, not separate TIME columns.
## ROUND, CEIL, FLOOR and rounding behaviour
ROUND(x, n) rounds to n decimal places, CEIL/CEILING rounds up, and FLOOR rounds down. To cut off digits without rounding, use TRUNCATE(x, n) in MySQL, TRUNC(x, n) in PostgreSQL, and ROUND(x, n, 1) in SQL Server. What matters for testers is that different systems round halves differently:

| Value | SQL ROUND (exact numbers, MySQL/PG) |
|---|---|
| Python round() | JavaScript Math.round() |

- Equality depends on collation: case, accent and trailing-space handling differ across MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server; check the real collation instead of assuming.
- Force behaviour with COLLATE (MySQL utf8mb4_bin, SQL Server ..._CS_AS), LOWER(), or PG's ILIKE.
- Case-insensitive uniqueness and near-duplicate emails are real defects to test; normalize with LOWER(TRIM()) when checking.
- LIKE wildcards: % and _; escape them to match literally (backslash default in MySQL/PG, ESCAPE clause, or brackets in SQL Server).
- Search boxes: try %, _, \, ', spaces, mixed case; unescaped input returning everything is a bug, and a quote error hints at injection risk.
- Leading wildcards (LIKE '%x') prevent index use; regex is REGEXP (MySQL), ~ (PG), none in SQL Server.
- Invisible differences (spaces, non-breaking spaces, tabs, CR/LF, zero-width and lookalike characters) break matches; inspect with HEX(), compare CHAR_LENGTH vs LENGTH, and search with name <> TRIM(name) or regex.
- Character sets: MySQL utf8 is 3-byte, so emoji need utf8mb4; watch for ???? and double-encoded text; test Devanagari end to end.
- Avoid comparing numeric text to numbers; stay in one type.
- Checklist for matched or unique fields: case, spaces, pasted characters, accents, apostrophes, % _ \ ', Unicode, max length, and compare the UI with the raw database.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Text comparison is more complicated than it looks
WHERE name = 'Ravi' seems unambiguous, but what it matches depends on the column's collation, the set of rules that decide when two strings are equal and how they sort. Collation controls case sensitivity, accent sensitivity, whether trailing spaces count, and how characters rank. Different databases ship with different defaults, and a table can override them, so "works on my machine" bugs are common here. Search boxes, login lookups, duplicate detection and imports all depend on it.
Using our scratch table, the rows are: 'Ravi', 'ravi', 'RAVI', 'Ravi ' (trailing space), ' Ravi' (leading space), 'Rávi' (accent), and 'Ravi' followed by a non-breaking space (the last row looks identical to the first on screen). Now WHERE name = 'Ravi' on each database's typical defaults:

| Database (typical default) | Rows matched by name = 'Ravi' |
|---|---|
| MySQL 8 (utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci: case- and accent-insensitive, trailing spaces significant) | Ravi, ravi, RAVI, Rávi |
| PostgreSQL (case- and accent-sensitive, trailing spaces significant) | Ravi only |
| SQL Server (..._CI_AS: case-insensitive, accent-sensitive, trailing spaces ignored) | Ravi, ravi, RAVI, Ravi |

Three databases, three answers to the same query, and none of them match the leading-space row or the non-breaking-space row. Older MySQL versions and collations like utf8mb4_general_ci ignore trailing spaces, too. Defaults vary by version and how the database was created, so check the actual collation instead of trusting a table like this:
```sql
-- MySQL
```
| SHOW FULL COLUMNS FROM text_demo;                       -- Collation column | SELECT @@collation_database; | -- PostgreSQL |
|---|---|---|
| SELECT datcollate FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database(); | -- SQL Server | SELECT DATABASEPROPERTYEX('hrms_qa', 'Collation'); |

Forcing case-sensitive or case-insensitive comparison
When you need a specific behaviour regardless of the column default:
```sql
-- MySQL: exact, case- and accent-sensitive
SELECT id, name FROM text_demo WHERE name = 'ravi' COLLATE utf8mb4_bin;    -- id 2 only
```

```sql
-- PostgreSQL: case-insensitive comparison
SELECT id, name FROM text_demo WHERE LOWER(name) = 'ravi';
-- or with ILIKE (PostgreSQL only)
SELECT id, name FROM text_demo WHERE name ILIKE 'ravi';
```

```sql
-- SQL Server: case-sensitive
SELECT id, name FROM text_demo WHERE name = 'ravi' COLLATE Latin1_General_CS_AS;
```

Applying LOWER() to the column works but is not sargable (2.1). Where speed matters, a case-insensitive collation or a functional index is better.
## Why this matters for testing: uniqueness and login
Is Asha@example.com a duplicate of asha@example.com? In a case-insensitive database with a unique index on email, the second insert fails. In a case-sensitive one, both are stored, and you now have two accounts that a user would consider the same, and a login lookup that may pick either. Test both the constraint and the app's behaviour, and query for near-duplicates directly:
```sql
SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS normalized, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM   employees
GROUP  BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```

(GROUP BY/HAVING are covered in 3.2; the point is the LOWER(TRIM(...)) normalisation.)
## LIKE, wildcards and escaping
LIKE matches patterns with two wildcards: % for "any number of characters" (including none) and _ for "exactly one character."
WHERE email LIKE 'a%'        -- starts with a
WHERE email LIKE '%@example.com'   -- ends with the domain
WHERE name  LIKE '%av%'      -- contains "av"
## WHERE name  LIKE 'R_vi'      -- R, any one character, vi

The gotcha is data that contains % or _. Our scratch table has 'Ram_Bahadur' and '100% Pass'. An unescaped LIKE 'Ram_Bahadur' would also match 'RamXBahadur', and LIKE '100% Pass' would match '1000 Pass' and '100 anything Pass'. Escape the wildcard to match it literally:
```sql
-- MySQL / PostgreSQL: backslash is the default escape character
SELECT * FROM text_demo WHERE name LIKE 'Ram\_Bahadur';
SELECT * FROM text_demo WHERE name LIKE '100\% Pass';
```

-- Portable everywhere (choose your own escape character)
```sql
SELECT * FROM text_demo WHERE name LIKE 'Ram!_Bahadur' ESCAPE '!';
```

```sql
-- SQL Server also allows bracket escaping
SELECT * FROM text_demo WHERE name LIKE 'Ram[_]Bahadur';
```

SQL Server has no default escape character, so always add ESCAPE or use brackets there.
This is a fruitful area for bug hunting, because many apps build a search from user input like WHERE name LIKE '%' + input + '%' without escaping. Type % or _ into the search box: a correct app treats them as literal characters, a naive one returns every row. Typing a single quote (') tests whether the input is parameterized or breaks the query, which leads into SQL injection (9.7).
A search-box test in Playwright, comparing the UI to a correctly escaped DB query:
```ts
const escapeLike = (s: string) => s.replace(/[\\%_]/g, '\\$&');
```

for (const term of ['ravi', 'RAVI', ' ravi ', '100%', 'Ram_', "O'Brien", '%']) {
| test(`search "${term}" matches DB`, async ({ page }) => { | await page.getByPlaceholder('Search').fill(term); |
|---|---|
| await page.keyboard.press('Enter'); | const uiCount = await page.locator('table tbody tr').count(); |

```ts
    const [rows]: any = await db.execute(
      'SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM text_demo WHERE name LIKE ?',
      [`%${escapeLike(term.trim())}%`]);   // requirement: literal, trimmed, case-insensitive contains
```

    expect(uiCount).toBe(rows[0].n);
  });
}

The test encodes the requirement ("contains, literal, trimmed") as the DB query. If the UI returns everything for %, the count mismatch flags it.
## Leading wildcards and performance
LIKE 'Rav%' (wildcard at the end) can use an index because the start of the string is known. LIKE '%avi' (wildcard at the start) can't, so it scans the table. If a search feels slow on big tables, a contains-style search may be the cause, and real "search" features often move to full-text search instead. Worth knowing when you file a performance issue.
## Regular expressions
For patterns that LIKE can't express, MySQL and PostgreSQL offer regex, and SQL Server doesn't (it has only limited LIKE character classes):
```sql
-- MySQL
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE email REGEXP '^[a-z0-9._]+@example\\.com$';
-- PostgreSQL
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE email ~ '^[a-z0-9._]+@example\.com$';
-- SQL Server (approximation using LIKE classes)
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE email LIKE '%[^a-z0-9._@]%';   -- contains an unexpected character
```

Negating the pattern gives you a "find invalid data" query, for example emails that don't match the expected shape.
## Whitespace, invisible characters and lookalikes
The biggest cause of "these two values look identical but don't match" is invisible difference. Typical culprits:
Leading or trailing spaces (from copy-paste or imports).
Non-breaking spaces (character code 160), common in text copied from web pages and Word, which TRIM doesn't remove (it removes ordinary spaces only).
Tabs, line feeds and carriage returns (\t, \n, \r), especially in imported CSV data with Windows line endings.
Zero-width characters (invisible, zero length).
Lookalike characters, such as a Cyrillic а in place of a Latin a.
Composed vs decomposed accents (é as one character vs e plus a combining mark), which some collations treat as equal and binary comparison doesn't.
To see what's really there, look at the bytes:
```sql
SELECT id, name, CHAR_LENGTH(name) AS chars, LENGTH(name) AS bytes, HEX(name) AS hex_bytes
FROM   text_demo
WHERE  name LIKE 'Ravi%';
```

id | name  | chars | bytes | hex_bytes
| 1  \| Ravi  \| 4     \| 4     \| 52617669 | 2  \| ravi  \| 4     \| 4     \| 72617669 | 3  \| RAVI  \| 4     \| 4     \| 52415649 |
|---|---|---|
| 4  \| Ravi  \| 5     \| 5     \| 5261766920 | 6  \| Rávi  \| 4     \| 5     \| 52C3A16976 | 9  \| Ravi  \| 5     \| 6     \| 52617669C2A0 |

Row 4's extra 20 is a space. Row 9's C2A0 is the non-breaking space, invisible on screen and impossible to see in most result grids. Row 6 shows the character/byte difference (4 vs 5) from the accent. PostgreSQL's equivalent is encode(convert_to(name, 'UTF8'), 'hex'), and SQL Server's is CONVERT(VARBINARY(100), name).
To hunt these down at scale:
-- Values with leading/trailing regular spaces
```sql
SELECT id, name FROM text_demo WHERE name <> TRIM(name);
```

-- Values containing anything outside printable ASCII (MySQL)
```sql
SELECT id, name FROM text_demo WHERE name REGEXP '[^ -~]';
```

-- Values where byte length differs from character length (multi-byte characters present)
```sql
SELECT id, name FROM text_demo WHERE LENGTH(name) <> CHAR_LENGTH(name);
```

Run checks like these against columns that feed matching logic: emails, employee codes, usernames, lookup names. Nearly any imported or migrated data (6.1) can contain such characters.
## Character sets and Unicode
A character set decides which characters a column can store. In MySQL, the old utf8 is really a 3-byte subset (utf8mb3) and can't store emoji or some rarer characters, which need utf8mb4. Inserting them fails with an "Incorrect string value" error (or is silently mangled in non-strict mode). If your product supports Nepali (Devanagari) names or user-entered emoji, always test them end to end: enter the text in the UI, look at the raw bytes in the database, and check it renders correctly when read back through the API. Signs of encoding problems are ???? (data lost on write) or à¤¨... sequences (data double-encoded: written as UTF-8 but read as Latin-1).
## Comparing text to numbers
If a column holds numeric-looking text (like employee_code = '007'), comparing it to a number makes the database convert one side, and MySQL's leniency gets you surprises: '007' = 7 is true and 'abc' = 0 is also true (with a warning). Stay in one type: compare text to text (employee_code = '007') or cast on purpose. Sorting numeric text is alphabetical ('10' before '9'), as covered in 1.2.
## A short text-testing checklist
For any field that the app matches, searches, or enforces as unique, try: different case, leading/trailing spaces, a pasted value with a non-breaking space, an accented letter, a name with an apostrophe (O'Brien), the characters %, _, \, and ', Devanagari and emoji, and a string right at the column's maximum length. Then look at both what the app shows and what the database holds. The gap between the two is where these bugs live.
